standard.title: Halves, quarters and eighths
standard.description: recognise and describe one-half as one of 2 equal parts of a whole and connect halves, quarters and eighths through repeated halving
standard.prior_knowledge: Students have informally explored equal sharing (AC9M1N06). They have not yet named halves, quarters or eighths as unit fractions, or connected them through the structure of repeated halving.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students recognise one-half as one of two equal parts of a whole, and connect halves, quarters and eighths by demonstrating and explaining repeated halving across shapes, objects and collections.

nodes.label: One-half as equal parts
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify and create one-half of a shape, object or collection, explaining that both parts must be equal.
nodes.minimum_width: Share a collection or fold a shape into 2 equal parts; identify one part as one-half; confirm equality of the two parts.
nodes.typical_width: Create halves of shapes, objects and collections using different methods (folding, measuring, sharing); explain 'a half is one part out of 2 equal parts of a whole'; compare halves of different-sized wholes.
wider: Compare half of a set of 12 counters with half of a set of 8 counters — discuss how both are one-half even though they are different amounts
Create halves using measurement contexts: half of a strip of paper, half of a cup of water; explain what 'equal' means in each case
nodes.hinge_reason: Nodes 2 and 3 depend on halving — creating quarters by halving a half, and eighths by halving a quarter. Students who accept unequal parts as halves will produce incorrect quarters and eighths, and the repeated-halving structure breaks completely.

response_modes.reason: Students commonly confuse half with 'one of two parts' without understanding the equal-parts constraint, and conflate the size of the half with the concept of one-half (e.g. thinking half of 12 is bigger than half of 8, so it's 'more than a half'). Multiple contexts — shapes, objects and collections — help students see that the relationship (1 of 2 equal parts) is what defines one-half, not the size.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Comparing halves of different-sized wholes is genuinely rich — it surfaces the relational nature of fractions and connects to proportional reasoning emerging at this year level. Advancing students can articulate why half of 12 ≠ half of 8 in absolute terms, yet both are one-half of their respective whole.
success_criteria: Creates or identifies one-half of a shape, object or collection with equal parts
Explains that both halves must be equal — not just two parts

nodes.label: Quarters through repeated halving
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can create quarters by halving a half, and name each part as one-quarter.
nodes.minimum_width: Fold or divide a shape or object in half, then fold the half in half again; name each of the four equal parts as one-quarter.
nodes.typical_width: Create quarters of shapes, objects and collections using repeated halving; demonstrate that a quarter is a half of a half; name parts and compare sizes.
wider: Investigate how food items (sandwiches, pizzas, slices) can be cut into quarters by halving twice; confirm all parts are equal
Explore halves and quarters in real measurement contexts: half a cup, quarter of a metre length, half an hour
success_criteria: Creates quarters by halving a half using a material or shape
Names each of the four equal parts as one-quarter and confirms they are equal in size

nodes.label: Eighths through repeated halving
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can create eighths by halving a quarter, explain that an eighth is a half of a quarter, and compare the sizes of halves, quarters and eighths of the same whole.
nodes.minimum_width: Divide a shape or strip into eighths by repeated halving; name each part as one-eighth; state that an eighth is a half of a quarter.
nodes.typical_width: Create and name halves, quarters and eighths through repeated halving; compare the size of parts (eighths are smaller than quarters, quarters are smaller than halves); relate number of parts to the size of each part.
wider: Use repeated halving to subdivide shapes in different ways; discuss why the more times you halve, the smaller each part becomes
Divide a shape into 4 equal parts and 8 equal parts; compare one-quarter and one-eighth; connect to the unit fraction rule (4 equal parts → one-quarter; 8 equal parts → one-eighth)

response_modes.reason: This node brings together halves, quarters and eighths as a connected structure. The key integration is the inverse relationship: more equal parts means each part is smaller. Students need to coordinate the part-count, the name, and the size simultaneously.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The generalisation that 'more equal parts → smaller each part' is a foundational fraction concept with genuine richness. Advancing students can articulate this as a principle and apply it to predict relative sizes (e.g. is one-third bigger or smaller than one-quarter?).
success_criteria: Creates eighths by repeated halving and names each part as one-eighth
States that an eighth is smaller than a quarter and a quarter is smaller than a half of the same whole
Explains the relationship: a quarter is a half of a half; an eighth is a half of a quarter
